prs.title: perf(turbo-persistence): shard meta files by family
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

- Store live meta files in primary per-family shards so queries avoid unrelated-family metadata.
- Keep compaction metadata incremental: replacement meta files describe only merged/moved SSTs, while fully consumed old meta files retire in the same commit. Used-key marks intentionally decay instead of being copied forward.
- Add debug assertions for shard ownership and within-family ordering invariants.

## Performance

Paired `LARGE_DB=1` Criterion binaries were run interleaved on the same machine after rebasing onto the per-family-compression change.

| Scenario | Canary | PR | Result |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Four-family cached `get` miss (100 metas/family) | 3.69–3.74 µs | 2.80–2.92 µs | **~23% faster** |
| Existing single-family cached `get` miss | 2.51–2.74 µs | 2.61–2.70 µs | Neutral across paired rounds |
| Existing full compaction (4 Mi entries, 8 commits) | ~1.12 s | ~1.12 s | Neutral across paired rounds |

Read hits stop at the newest matching meta, so their improvement is too small to measure; misses are the primary benefit because they previously scanned every family.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p turbo-persistence`
- `cargo test -p turbo-persistence --features stats`
- `cargo clippy -p turbo-persistence --all-targets --features stats -- -D warnings`
- `LARGE_DB=1` interleaved Criterion A/B runs

prs.title: docs: rewrite the bots and crawlers section in the caching guide
prs.author: icyJoseph
prs.body:
## Summary

The Bots and crawlers section in the caching guide said that all bots and crawlers skip the static shell because "they need a complete document". Only HTML-limited bots do, and the reason is metadata: with Partial Prerendering, `generateMetadata` can resolve dynamically and stream in after the shell, which puts the tags in the body rather than the `<head>`. Bots that need them in the `<head>` get a dynamic render instead.

The second paragraph now states the consequence directly: if the build-time prerender read something unreachable at request time, the render throws and those bots get a 500. Which user agents this covers, and the `htmlLimitedBots` option for changing the list, stay owned by the Streaming guide, which the section links to.

prs.title: Keep metadata rendering stable across streaming modes
prs.author: gnoff
prs.body:
## Motivation

Streaming and blocking metadata previously used different rendering paths. Metadata placement should depend on when Next.js starts consuming the response, rather than requiring the metadata component itself to render outside Suspense.

## What this does

Selected metadata now always renders through the same hidden Suspense boundary. For blocking responses, an always-present `MetadataBlocker` waits for the same cached resolution before Next.js pulls the response, ensuring metadata remains in the document head.

`MetadataOutlet` remains a single promise. It renders inside Suspense for streaming responses and outside Suspense for blocking responses so navigation and regular errors retain their existing behavior.

HTML-limited bot requests continue to bypass PPR shells. A prerendered shell has already closed its head before dynamic metadata resolves, so resuming that shell cannot provide blocking metadata in the raw head.

## Review notes

- Metadata resolution still starts from a rendered component so the active `workUnitStore` and React cache scope are available.
- Fizz may begin rendering before metadata settles; blocking is enforced before Next.js starts pulling the response.
- The hidden wrapper keeps top-level suspenseful metadata out of the document preamble. Metadata tags hoist out, so the wrapper remains empty.
- The Cache Components blocking and hydration coverage runs with parallel metadata both disabled and enabled.

## Verification

- `pnpm build-all`
- `pnpm test-start-turbo test/e2e/app-dir/metadata-streaming-cache-components/metadata-streaming-cache-components-custom-bots.test.ts`
- `pnpm test-start-webpack test/e2e/app-dir/metadata-streaming-cache-components/metadata-streaming-cache-components-custom-bots.test.ts`

prs.title: [PPF] Fix unnecessary runtime prefetch with prefetch={true}
prs.author: lubieowoce
prs.body:
In, we #98278 attempted to fix runtime follow-ups for shells (if a static prefetch produced an insuffient shell).

However, it introduced a regression in this scenario, where neither shells or prefetches use runtime data, so both of these links should use static prefetches:
```tsx
<Link href="/static-param/one" prefetch={true} />
{/* Revealed later */}
<Link href="/static-param/two" prefetch={true} />
```

We'd correctly do a static prefetch for the first link. However, the second link would see a `RuntimeShell`-tier shell from the first link, and this check inside `isShellEntryEligibleForStaticAttempt` would fail (because `RuntimeShell` was now greater than `PPR`):
https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/3c9d1ca77f7de845315dc166a57fc9f090c638b4/packages/next/src/client/components/segment-cache/scheduler.ts#L1261
as a result, `isShellEntryEligibleForStaticAttempt` would return `false`, and we would deopt to a runtime prefetch for the second link instead.

Importantly, a page with `ensureStatic = "prefetch"`(which will be implemented in #98191) will currently be handled exactly like a page that did not use runtime data at build -- the client doesn't know that a page is meant to never use runtime requests at all, it's entirely based on the existing static hints/`needsRuntimeRequest` promise mechanism. So even if `/static/[slug]` sets `ensureStatic = "prefetch"`, we'd also do an unnecessary runtime prefetch for it even though we really shouldn't. Violating the `ensureStatic` contract seems worse than a missing runtime shell follow-up , because those can currently only happen if the shell starts using runtime data after a revalidation, and that's probably not a common scenario. So i'm partially reverting that change until we figure out how to handle this in a way that handles both cases correctly (i've attempted doing that, but it seems nontrivial)

We're now missing the runtime shell follow-up again, so tests related to that in `prefetch-app-shell-revalidation.test.ts` are marked as failing (but still assert on current behavior -- the follow-up failures can be reproduced by setting `REPRODUCE_MISSING_RUNTIME_SHELL_FOLLOW_UP=1`).

prs.title: Replace lzzzz with lz4_flex
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## What?

Replace the direct `lzzzz` dependency used by Turbopack persistence with `lz4_flex` 0.14. The migration covers persisted blocks, the SST inspection utility, and optional compressed-size diagnostics in the task backend.

## Why?

This removes the direct C/liblz4-backed codec dependency from these paths in favor of a Rust implementation. Persistence caches are scoped to the Next.js and Turbopack version, so this does not require a compatibility path for caches written by earlier versions.

## How?

Persistence continues to use raw LZ4 blocks and the existing compression selection and checksum layout.

A large thread-local `CompressTable` is reused across blocks. Starting with the large table costs about 8 KiB more per compression thread than the small table, but improves compression speed and produces LZ4 streams that are faster for `lz4_flex` to decode.

The compressor retains the existing caller-owned buffer API. It clears and reserves the output vector, lets `lz4_flex` write directly into the uninitialized backing allocation, and exposes only the initialized byte count returned by the compressor. This avoids both per-call output allocations and pre-zeroing the maximum output size. Zstandard behavior is unchanged.

### Benchmark vs `lzzzz`

The final PR configuration was benchmarked against `lzzzz` 2.0.0 using the repository-pinned Rust nightly. The benchmark used source-code blocks sampled from this repository, pinned each process to one physical CPU, measured thread CPU time, and alternated codec order within every paired round. The table reports the median across four physical cores and 20 paired rounds per process (480 paired rounds total).

Each decoder read the output produced by its own encoder, matching how a same-version persistence cache is written and later read.

| Mixed | 16 KiB | **5.9% faster** | 8.8% slower | 0.17% smaller |
| Rust | 16 KiB | **4.6% faster** | 10.0% slower | 0.12% smaller |
| TypeScript | 16 KiB | **6.7% faster** | 6.1% slower | 0.02% smaller |

prs.title: Keep guards across restore owner handoff
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Prevent eviction or GC from clearing a task while the thread that restored it hands the task back to its caller.

This is the first open layer in stack #98709. The construction-time GC pin it builds on has already landed through #98688.

### Why?

A restore clears the category's `restoring` bit while still holding the task lock. The old code then dropped that lock so it could notify waiters without making them immediately contend on the same shard, and finally re-acquired the task guard for its caller.

That creates a small but real gap: once the restoring bit is clear and the lock is dropped, the task is considered evictable. Concurrent eviction can remove the category before the restoring thread re-acquires it. The restore then returns a task that no longer contains the data it just loaded, leading to stale task references, missing task types, or incorrect values.

The same interleaving exists for both single-task restoration and paired task access.

### How?

Keep the existing task guard through `restored.notify(...)` and return that same guard directly. Pair access likewise retains both guards through notification.

Notification only wakes listeners; it does not acquire task locks or wait for listeners to run, so retaining the guard cannot deadlock. Woken waiters may briefly contend until the restoring call returns, but there is no longer any unguarded interval in which eviction or GC can clear the newly restored category.

This layer introduces no new state or pin accounting. The complementary waiter-side handoff is isolated in #98728.

### Verification

- `cargo test -p turbo-tasks-backend --lib` (102 passed)
- `cargo test -p turbo-tasks-backend --test eviction --test gc_resurrection --test gc_collection --test gc_interrupt --test gc_stress` (19 passed)
- `cargo fmt -- --check`
- `cargo clippy -p turbo-tasks-backend --tests -- -D warnings`

Built on the construction pin merged in #98688. Followed by #98728.

prs.title: test: run cargo unit tests with miri as well
prs.author: mischnic
prs.body:
### What?

Adds a CI job that runs selected Rust unit tests under [Miri](https://github.com/rust-lang/miri) to detect undefined behavior in unsafe code.

The job currently covers the low-level crates that are compatible with Miri:

- `turbo-persistence`
- `turbo-rcstr`
- `turbo-tasks-malloc`

It also makes those crates Miri-compatible by:

- using provenance-free tagged-pointer operations in `turbo-rcstr`;
- disabling mimalloc and native compression under Miri;
- making mmap support a default-enabled Cargo feature that is disabled for Miri and wasm;
- running persistence through file I/O when mmap is disabled;
- skipping only tests measured to exceed the Miri time budget;
- removing leaked test arenas from the analyzer predicate tests.

### Why?

Miri can detect invalid memory access and other undefined behavior that normal Rust tests may not expose. Running it in CI gives low-level unsafe code an additional correctness check.

The job uses an explicit package allowlist because Turbo Tasks builds its generated registry from linker sections, and Miri does not support the linker-defined section symbols required by that registry.

### How?

prs.title: example(cache-handler-redis): fix connection leak, hangs on a down Redis, and cross-page tag invalidation
prs.author: leejpsd
prs.body:
Three runtime problems in `examples/cache-handler-redis`.

### 1. One new Redis connection per request, never closed

Next.js constructs the singular `cacheHandler` class once per request (`new CurCacheHandler(...)` in `IncrementalCache`, which `route-module.ts` creates per request). The example's constructor calls `createClient()` + `connect()`, so every request opens a connection that is never closed.

```
$ redis-cli client list | wc -l      # before
102
$ for i in $(seq 1 10); do curl -s -o /dev/null localhost:3000/cet; done
$ redis-cli client list | wc -l
132                                  # +3 per request
```

With Redis' default `maxclients 10000`, a single instance runs out after a few thousand requests.

### 2. Requests hang while Redis is unavailable

The README says the handlers "degrade gracefully when Redis is unavailable, so the app still builds and runs, just without a shared cache". At runtime they don't: with Redis stopped, every request on every instance blocks until Redis comes back.

```
$ docker stop cache-handler-redis
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -m 60 -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" localhost:3000/cet
000 60.007305s                       # (uncapped: 188s, returned the moment Redis was started again)
```

Same when the app is started while Redis is down. Cause: node-redis keeps retrying in the background and `client.connect()` does not settle until a connection succeeds. Isolated:

```js
const c = createClient({ url: "redis://localhost:6379" }); c.on("error", () => {});
await Promise.race([c.connect(), new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r("pending"), 15000))]);
// -> "pending" after 15s, isOpen=true isReady=false   (redis@6.2.1)
```

Because each request built a new handler, each request awaited a fresh, never-settling `connect()` in `getClient()`. `remote-cache-handler.js` has one module-level client, but its `getClient()` awaits the same promise, so it hangs the same way if the app starts while Redis is down.

### 3. `updateTag` never reaches other pages' remote entries

The remote handler's `get` never checks the entry's own tags. Next.js only passes soft tags to `getExpiration`, and the `"use cache"` wrapper only knows about tags revalidated in the current request, so `updateTag("time-data")` from `/cet` left the `/gmt` entry stale on every instance, including the one that ran it, until it expired (`cacheLife` `expire: 3600`). The [`cacheHandlers` docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers#get) say `get` should report an entry whose tag was invalidated as missing or stale.

### Fix

- Hoist the client in `cache-handler.js` to module scope (the pattern `remote-cache-handler.js` already uses).
- `getClient()` awaits the connect promise raced against a 1s `unref()`'d timer (suggested in review), then returns the client when `isReady` and `null` otherwise. Requests during startup still wait for the connection, and a down Redis costs one bounded wait instead of blocking every request. 
…(truncated)

prs.title: Pin tasks across restore waiter handoff
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Keep a task alive across the restore-waiter handoff: from the moment a caller observes another thread restoring a category until that caller acquires the restored task for use.

This is the first open layer in stack #98709. The construction and restore-owner races have already landed in `canary` through #98688 and #98700.

### Why?

The `restoring` bits elect exactly one thread to perform backing-storage I/O. A waiting caller observes that ownership under the task lock, drops the lock, and then holds only a `TaskId` while waiting for notification. That temporary in-session reference is not represented by a parent or aggregation edge, so GC may otherwise collect the task after the restorer clears its bit but before the waiter acquires a guard.

Eviction is different: it is safe for eviction to clear the completed restore in this window as long as the waiter does not mistake that state for an I/O failure. The waiter can claim the now-unowned category and restore it again.

Batch preparation has the same task-id-outside-the-graph interval between classification and callback. Pair access needs both task IDs kept alive until both guards can be acquired together.

### How?

Each waiting caller increments the existing `transient_ref_count` before dropping the task lock and decrements exactly one ref under the guard at its actual use boundary. This uses the GC-root mechanism and invariant checks that already protect construction, transient-parent, and detached-handle references.

The transient ref does not block value eviction. If a waiter observes a category that is neither restored nor currently restoring, it keeps its GC pin, claims the category, and performs another restore. A replacement restorer retains its acquired guard through notification and returns that same still-pinned guard to the caller.

Successful pin release belongs entirely to the caller:

- single-task access releases after receiving the restored guard;
- pair access releases after acquiring both guards together;
- batch preparation releases immediately before passing the guard to its callback.

The helper decrements the ref itself only on `Err`, where no guard is returned. The already-restored fast path remains and avoids listener registration.

This removes the dedicated handoff field and eviction blocker. It also keeps `gc_maybe_collectible()` and `gc_debug_assert_root_held_by_transient_pin()` aligned on the same existing transient-ref predicate.

### Verification

- Latest `origin/canary` (`389f164d`) in a detached worktree
- `cargo test -p turbo-tasks-backend --lib` (102 passed)
- `cargo test -p turbo-tasks-backend --test eviction --test gc_resurrection --test gc_collection --test gc_interrupt --test gc_stress` (19 passed)
- Eviction-permitting stress: 0 failures across 1,200 runs using 8 parallel workers
- Sequential stress: 0 failures across 150 runs
- `cargo fmt -- --check`
- `cargo clippy -p turbo-tasks-backend --tests -- -D warnings`

Followed by #98729.

prs.title: Persist resurrected tasks as new tasks
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Ensure a GC-resurrected persistent task is persisted again as a new task.

This is the final layer in stack #98709 and depends on the restore-waiter lifetime fix in #98728.

### Why?

GC soft-deletes a disconnected task, then the following snapshot persists a tombstone that removes its durable task record and task-type lookup entry. Normal operations resume after the snapshot's logical state is frozen, so a concurrent connection can still find the resident soft-deleted task and resurrect it before post-snapshot eviction removes the in-memory entry.

Resurrection already cleared `deleted`, marked the task dirty, and scheduled recomputation. It did not, however, mark the task as newly publishable. If the tombstone had already committed, later snapshots could persist recomputed data without re-establishing the complete persistent identity of the resurrected task. Once in-memory cache state was evicted, future lookups could no longer recover that otherwise-live task by type.

A resident deleted task is guaranteed to retain its type: GC restores all categories before marking it deleted, and post-snapshot eviction handles deleted tasks by removing the whole entry rather than partially dropping the type.

### How?

When the connect handshake wins the resurrection race, mark the task as `new_task` again and mark its Data category modified. The next snapshot therefore persists it using the normal new-task path, including recreating its task-type lookup entry and the Data record used to verify that lookup.

The task remains dirty so its cells and graph edges are rebuilt through the existing recomputation path. The update is unconditional for a resident deleted task; a missing type remains an invariant violation rather than being silently skipped.

### Verification

- Top-of-stack stress: 0 failures across 1,200 runs using 8 parallel workers
- Sequential stress: 0 failures across 150 runs
- `cargo test -p turbo-tasks-backend --lib` (102 passed)
- `cargo test -p turbo-tasks-backend --test eviction --test gc_resurrection --test gc_collection --test gc_interrupt --test gc_stress` (19 passed)

prs.title: Use structural React keys during server rendering
prs.author: gnoff
prs.body:
## Summary

Use structural React keys during server rendering so an HTML prerender can resume without rewriting React's postponed state when route params become known. Browser keys and router-cache identity are unchanged.

For example, `/products/[slug]` previously prerendered layout boundaries with a key containing an opaque slug placeholder. Resuming `/products/shoe` produced a different key, so Next.js substituted `shoe` into the serialized React state before handing it back to React. Both server passes now use `slug|d`. The browser still uses `slug|shoe|d`, preserving template remounts and back/forward state behavior.

The server only renders the active entry at each layout-router position, so it does not need parameter values to distinguish cached browser entries. React keys are not embedded in the HTML; hydration derives its concrete keys from the request's route state.

- Use segment name/type for server layout keys and structural route paths for the server head key. Server keys always omit search params. The existing browser-module variant mechanism selects the concrete key implementation for browser bundles in both Webpack and Turbopack.

- Simplify the remaining opaque fallback map to param name → placeholder. Its dynamic-param type slot is unused after removing interpolation. Parameter wrappers still control suspension; this does not make unknown params available to application code.
- Test server and browser keys directly, including catch-all/intercepted segments and search params. Update the action-only resume fixture's single assertion on the resume-metadata format so its three cases reach their behavioral checks for action execution, revalidation, and `notFound()` with names-only metadata.

```text
├── layout.tsx
├── @left/foo/page.tsx
└── @right/bar/page.tsx
```

prs.title: fix(turbo-persistence): preserve write errors on writer drop
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Preserve write failures from streaming SST construction instead of replacing them with debug-only writer lifecycle assertions. This adds explicit cancellation, immediate best-effort cleanup of incomplete SSTs, and focused coverage for failed writes and finalization.

### Why?

`std::thread::panicking()` is false while an error is propagated through `Result`. On disk-full and similar failures, writers and their owning collectors are therefore dropped before a caller begins panic unwinding, allowing lifecycle assertions to obscure the original I/O error. Leaving partial files until startup recovery also delays reclaiming scarce disk space.

### How?

`StreamingSstWriter::cancel()` consumes an incomplete writer, discards buffered bytes without flushing or finalizing, closes the raw handle, and best-effort removes the partial SST. Failed close attempts and unfinished Drop paths use the same cleanup, while deletion failures are ignored so they cannot replace the root error; existing startup recovery remains the fallback.

Writer-owning scopes preserve the original error, explicitly cancel their writers, and then return that error. The compaction merge scope cancels both collectors on every error exit so a sibling collector cannot mask the failure. Successful close marks the finalized SST for preservation, and healthy writers still have to call `close()` or `cancel()` to satisfy the debug lifecycle invariant.

The regression tests substitute an unbuffered read-only output handle to force deterministic add and close failures without requiring disk pressure.

### Verification

prs.title: feat(turbopack): support `false` values for `resolveAlias` config
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Adds support for `false` as a value in `experimental.turbopack.resolveAlias`, which resolves the aliased module to an empty stub — matching webpack's long-standing behavior.

```js
// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  experimental: {
    turbopack: {
      resolveAlias: {
        'some-server-only-module': false,
      },
    },
  },
}
```

With this alias in place:
- `import * as ns from 'some-server-only-module'` → `ns` is `{}`
- `import { foo } from 'some-server-only-module'` → `foo` is `undefined`
- `import def from 'some-server-only-module'` → `def` is `undefined`
- `await import('some-server-only-module')` → resolves to `{}`
- `require('some-server-only-module')` → returns `{}`

### Why?

Webpack supports `false` as an alias target to stub out modules (e.g. to exclude Node-only packages from client/edge bundles). Turbopack did not, causing migration friction for projects that rely on this pattern.

### How?

Threads the `false` sentinel through the full resolution pipeline as a new `Empty` variant:

```
false (config)
  → SubpathValue::Empty      (next-core import map)
  → ImportMapping::Empty     (turbopack-core remap)
  → ReplacedImportMapping::Empty
  → ResolveResultItem::Empty
  → ModuleResolveResultItem::Empty
  → ReferencedAsset::Empty   (ESM static imports)
  → SinglePatternMapping::Ignored  (CJS require / dynamic import)
```

For static ESM imports, `ReferencedAsset::Empty` is kept as a distinct variant so that `binding.rs` can distinguish a namespace import (yields `{}`) from a named/default import (yields `undefined`).

For CJS `require()` and dynamic `import()`, `ModuleResolveResultItem::Empty` maps to the existing `SinglePatternMapping::Ignored`, which already generates the correct `{}` / `Promise.resolve({})` stubs — so no new code-generation path was needed there (the redundant `Empty` variant introduced during development was removed in a follow-up cleanup commit).

prs.title: Turbopack: compact re-export registration
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## Summary

Adds a compact Turbopack runtime path for modules whose exports are entirely forwarded from other modules. It replaces one generated wrapper getter per binding with a flat re-export description, while preserving live-binding semantics and source evaluation order.

This revision also makes the optimization generic for synthetic re-export facades, rather than leaving facade integration in the stacked export-mangling PR:

- synthetic facades use `ExportRegistrationMode::Reexport`;
- their explicit reference list supplies ordering because they have no source `ImportMap`;
- an evaluation-only locals reference can be represented as an empty group;
- references whose import is performed by the compact registration do not emit it twice;
- pruned references and merged evaluation-only references are omitted, because they deliberately produce no namespace binding and may have no module factory in the chunk;
- async modules and known export-cycle circuit breakers retain the general registration path.

The runtime now inspects source property descriptors. Constant exports reuse the source value, live exports reuse the exact receiver-independent Turbopack namespace getter, and dynamic/proxy/missing properties fall back to a wrapper getter. Destination descriptors remain enumerable, non-configurable, read-only ESM namespace properties; setters are never forwarded.

## Output examples

A re-export-only module can suppress its redundant import and use a module-id group:

```js
// before
var ns = __turbopack_context__.i("a.js")
__turbopack_context__.s(["a", () => ns.a, "b", () => ns.b])

// after
__turbopack_context__.S(["a.js", "a,a,b,b"])
```

Two source modules become groups separated by `0`:

```js
__turbopack_context__.S([
  "first.js", "a,a,b,b",
  0,
  "second.js", "c,c",
])
```

Encoding is selected independently per group. A comma-containing name uses explicit pairs while another group can remain packed:

```js
__turbopack_context__.S([
  "first.js", "b", "b", "has,comma", "has,comma",
  0,
  "second.js", "c,c",
])
```

```js

  "reexports.js <locals>",
  0,
  "x.js", "x,x",
  0,
  "y.js", "y,y",
])
```

```js
__turbopack_context__.S([locals, 0, x, "x,x"], facadeId)
```

prs.title: perf: optimize CSS graph cycle removal
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

This PR changes how the graph-based CSS chunker resolves contradictory stylesheet ordering constraints.

The previous implementation repeatedly found one cycle, removed one edge from it, and searched again. On dense graphs this could repeat thousands of expensive searches over almost the same data.

The new implementation handles each cyclic region as a whole:

1. Compute a good global order for the modules in that region.
2. Improve that order with a small, bounded local search.
3. Remove every edge that disagrees with the chosen order in one pass.

This preserves the existing chunking pipeline and its hard constraints while making cycle removal much faster.

### Why?

A production reproduction contained:

- 499 CSS modules
- 104,473 directed ordering edges
- one cyclic region containing 475 modules
- 9,574 edges removed one at a time

`make_acyclic` alone took **9.61 seconds**. Each removed edge caused several weighted bidirectional shortest-path searches over nearly the same dense graph.

With this PR, the same reproduction spends **73.5 ms** in `make_acyclic` under full turbo-tasks tracing, approximately **131× faster** than the original measured phase.

### How does the CSS graph work?

This section intentionally avoids assuming graph-theory knowledge.

Suppose two routes import CSS in these orders:

```text
route A: reset.css, button.css, page-a.css
route B: reset.css, card.css, page-b.css
```

The chunker creates one node for each CSS file. For every ordered pair in a route, it records an arrow from the later file to the earlier file:

```text
button.css → reset.css
page-a.css → button.css
page-a.css → reset.css
```

An arrow means “the file on the left must come after the file on the right.” If several routes agree on the same relationship, the arrow gets a larger weight. The weight is therefore a vote count: a heavier arrow represents an ordering preference supported by more routes.

#### Why cycles appear

Different routes can disagree:

```text
route A: a.css, b.css
route B: b.css, a.css
```

That creates both:

```text
b.css → a.css
a.css → b.css
```

There is no global order that satisfies both. This is a cycle: following the arrows eventually returns to the starting node.

Before the graph can be converted into one linear CSS order, some contradictory arrows must be discarded. There is no universally correct choice in this situation because the input itself asks for mutually incompatible orders. The goal is to preserve as much heavily-supported ordering information as possible.

### Previous algorithm

The previous implementation:

1. Found a short cycle using weighted bidirectional Dijkstra searches.
2. Removed the lightest edge on that cycle.
3. Repeated until no cycle remained.

This makes intuitive sense for small graphs, but it is expensive when a dense cyclic region needs thousands of cuts: almost the same graph is searched again after every single removal.

prs.title: [PPF] Separate tracking of runtime data accesses for shells and prefetches
prs.author: lubieowoce
prs.body:
Expands the static tracking from #96095 to track shells and prefetches separately. We split the `ShouldAttemptStaticPrefetch` hint into `ShouldAttemptStaticShell` and `ShouldAttemptStaticPrefetch`, which the client router considers separately depending on whether we need a shell or a prefetch.

The server-side tracking of `needsRuntimeRequest` becomes a bit more subtle.

First, a runtime data access should only affect the shell if we're in the `ShellStatic` render stage. If we're already in the `PrefetchStatic` stage, then that content is not conceptually part of the shell, and should not deopt the shell to runtime, so we only unset `shouldAttemptStaticShell` if we're still in the shell stage.

Second, accessing data that would only resolve in the prefetch (params, search params, short-stale caches) should **not** affect whether the shell can be static. `makeRuntimeDataHangingPromise` has been split into variants that match this:
 - `makeSessionDataHangingPromise` - data that affects the shell (and the prefetch), e.g. `cookies()`
 - `makeURLDataHangingPromise` - data that only affects the prefetch, e.g. `params`
  - `makeUnknownRuntimeDataHangingPromise`, used for private caches -- we omit these during build so we don't know whether they should affect the shell or only the prefetch, so we conservatively affect both (unless a private cache is only used in the prefetch stage)

The server-side `needsRuntimeRequest` promise is now resolved such that data that only resolves in the prefetch does not affect the shell. If we're accessing data that only resolves in the prefetch, we will delay the promise's resolution to the `PrefetchStatic` stage, which means that when the client rewinds the static response to a shell, it will see an unresolved promise and consider the response as not having used runtime data. (see `markRuntimeDataAccessWhenStageReached`)

prs.title: Fix prefetch loop when a predicted route redirects
prs.author: acdlite
prs.body:
A full or runtime prefetch (e.g. `router.prefetch(url, { kind: 'full' })` or `<Link prefetch={true}>`) of a URL that matched a learned route pattern but is redirected by the server (e.g. `/docs/changelog` → `/changelog` while `/docs/alpha` renders `[collection]/[...slug]`) caused the client to re-issue the same prefetch indefinitely, at whatever rate the network allowed, until the tab was closed.

When the server contradicts a route prediction, the client is supposed to remember that the URL shape can't be predicted and resolve it on the server from then on. We were storing this information (`hasDynamicRewrite`) in the wrong place: on the predicted route cache entry, rather than the optimistic routing table that's used to generate predictions.

The fix moves the `hasDynamicRewrite` flag to the optimistic routing table so it applies to all subsequent optimistic routing predictions.

Fixes #98345.

prs.title: Don't re-request the App Shell to upgrade an ISR fallback
prs.author: acdlite
prs.body:
When a page hasn't been prerendered with concrete params yet, the server answers a per-segment prefetch with the fallback shell and flags it as upgradeable, and the client records that on the cache entries so a later prefetch of the same route can retry and pick up the concrete prerender once the server has generated it. The scheduler runs that retry from its Fulfilled-entry branch: any prefetch task that finds an upgradeable-fallback entry and hasn't retried yet spawns a revalidation for its own URL.

That's right for the concrete static walk, where the retry can bring back the param-dependent content the fallback omitted. It's wrong for the Shell-phase walk under Partial Prefetching. A shell request asks for shell-stage content, and the fallback render already produced all of it: a concrete prerender's shell stage omits the same param-dependent content the fallback omitted, so the retry can only return the shell the cache already has.

This shows up with root params. The shell varies only on the root params it reads, so a shell fetched for `/en/uk/posts/1` whose root layout reads `lang` but not `region` is keyed with `region` as a fallback, and a link to `/en/gb/posts/1` finds it in the cache. With the retry gate on, revealing that link re-requested the identical shell, once per link whose root params the shell doesn't read.

The fix gates the ISR fallback retry on the walk's strategy, next to the Pending and Rejected branches that already skip revalidations during a static shell attempt. The per-task retry loop that the original fallback response starts is unchanged.

The included test reveals three links from `/en/us`: `/en/uk/posts/1` fetches the shell, `/en/gb/posts/1` (same `lang`, different `region`) fetches nothing, and `/fr/uk/posts/1` (different `lang`) fetches a new shell.

This PR originally narrowed the shell's cache key to the root params the server reported. That change landed separately in "Convert per-segment prefetches to NavigationFlightResponse format" (#96877); rebasing onto it left the test, which then caught this.

### Why?

prs.title: Turbopack: mangle exports behind an escaping namespace via the facade
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Allows Turbopack to keep mangling a module's internal export keys when its namespace object escapes. A facade preserves the original public names while forwarding each one to the mangled key in the locals module, matching webpack's materialized-namespace behavior.

This PR is stacked on #98617. That lower PR now owns the generic synthetic-facade compact registration, including empty evaluation groups, descriptor reuse, scope-hoisted factories, pruned references, and cycle/async fallbacks. This PR creates those facades for escaping namespaces, so the generic path is exercised at scale here.

### Why?

A namespace import or dynamic import whose reads cannot be enumerated currently disables mangling for the entire target module. That makes one broad consumer lose the size benefit for every otherwise-static consumer of the module.

Materializing the original namespace surface keeps ESM semantics intact — including live values and `Object.keys()` — while allowing internal consumers to use shorter names.

### How?

The facade's synthesized per-export references participate in the module graph, so named usage propagates to the locals module. Its structural locals edge carries evaluation usage only, while each forwarded name carries its own export usage. Part-reference code generation also honors references pruned by the graph, matching ordinary ESM references.

Modules with no exports are not split, async modules retain the existing path, and real export-cycle circuit breakers avoid compact registration because they require their getters to be visible before imports run. Namespace grouping includes the SWC syntax context so scope-hoisted modules cannot accidentally share the wrong generated binding.

prs.title: test(turbo-tasks): run the wasm tests with a Node wasi host
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Adds a Node host so `wasm32-wasip1-threads` test binaries can run, and wires the `turbo-rcstr`, `turbo-tasks`, and `turbo-tasks-backend` library tests into the WASI CI job.

It also provides the WASI allocation symbols expected by the `lz4-sys` dependency introduced by the base PR, allowing those test binaries to link.

### Why?

The Rust test binaries require host functionality that stock WASI runners do not provide. Turbopack stores its link-time task registries in WebAssembly custom sections and imports a host callback to read them. Its multithreaded runtime also requires shared memory and thread spawning through Node Workers.

The base PR replaces `lzzzz` with `lz4`. `lz4-sys 1.11.1` compiles its C sources against custom allocation shims on `wasm32-wasi*`, but excludes the Rust implementations when the target OS is WASI. Without equivalent symbols supplied by the consuming crate, test links fail on unresolved malloc, calloc, and free shims.

Running these suites in CI gives the remaining WASI layers direct regression coverage instead of relying on native-only tests.

### How?

The Node cargo target runner provides WASI preview1, imported shared memory, and the complete two-phase [`link-section` custom-section protocol](https://github.com/mmastrac/linktime/blob/ae29e51d94a955df2442ed6418b8a712c1f2bfb3/link-section/docs/PREAMBLE.md#wasm).

[`@emnapi/wasi-threads`](https://github.com/toyobayashi/emnapi/tree/main/packages/wasi-threads) supplies Worker lifecycle, compiled-module transfer, load/start ordering, and cleanup for the [`wasi.thread-spawn`](https://github.com/WebAssembly/wasi-threads) import that Node's WASI runtime does not provide. The module is compiled once, then the structured-cloneable `WebAssembly.Module` and shared memory are sent to Workers. A small adapter around the package's lower-level `ThreadManager` and `ThreadMessageHandler` APIs preserves Rust's original one-argument ABI: the high-level `WASIThreads` wrapper requires guest `malloc`/`free` exports for that ABI, and Rust test binaries do not export them. Worker identifiers come from a shared atomic counter because Tokio Workers can spawn additional Workers while the main WebAssembly thread is parked.

On WASI, `turbo-persistence` supplies the three allocation symbols required by liblz4 and forwards them to WASI libc, keeping allocation and deallocation within the same allocator. Native builds do not compile these wrappers.

Tests that depend on unavailable platform behavior remain visible as WASI-only ignored tests with explicit reasons. Native runs keep the full test set enabled. A following stacked PR replaces the unsupported `parking_lot` parker and re-enables the corresponding contention tests.

The workflow installs and builds the workspace before running the host because both the package dependency and compiled production support used by a later stack layer must be available.

### Verification

- Node 20 host unit tests: 9/9
- Exact combined WASI CI comman

prs.title: [PPF] Validate `unstable_ensureStatic` nesting
prs.author: lubieowoce
prs.body:
`ensureStatic` forms a hierarchy: `"auto" < "shell" < "prefetch" < "navigation"`, with each value being more contrained than its predecessor.

1. A child segment cannot relax constraints set by a parent segment, it can only tighten them
    - so `shell` in a layout and `prefetch` in a page is fine, but the opposite is not
    - note that setting `"auto"` in the child *is* allowed, because it means "unconstrained" and is compatible with all the other configs
2. We can't have two conflicting levels set by two parallel slots (but `auto` is compatible with any other constraint, so it's allowed, same as above)
3. If a segment sets `ensureStatic = false`, then no other segments on that route are allowed to constrain the route by setting anything higher than `auto` (this is meant as a signal for e.g. "this segment DELIBERATELY uses a runtime shell and should not be overridden to be static")

Also adds exhaustive tests for all of these scenarios.

prs.title: [turbopack] Track members across namespace re-exports
prs.author: sampoder
prs.body:
## What?

This PR closes a missed tree-shaking opportunity for libraries that expose a module namespace as a named export. One real-world example is Zod, whose public API has a structure similar to the following (and this pattern also appears in v0's codebase):

```js
// user.js
import { z } from './lib.js'

console.log(z.object(), z.string(), z.defaultLocale)
```

```js
// lib.js — mirrors zod/index.js
import * as z from './external.js'

export * from './external.js'
export { z }
export default z

// external.js — mirrors zod/v4/classic/external.js
import en from './locales/en.js'

export * as locales from './locales/index.js'

export const object = () => 'object'
export const string = () => 'string'
export const defaultLocale = en
```

The analyzer can now preserve the information that only `object`, `string`, and `defaultLocale` are read from `z`, and use it after resolving that named export to the namespace of `external.js`.

This PR is now standalone on `canary`. Its two former prerequisites have landed: #98680 introduced the independently reviewed `EsmAssetReferenceOptions` constructor refactor, and #96282 integrated CommonJS and ESM whole-namespace forwarding with canary's generic `ExportUsage::Passthrough` fixed point.

## Why?

Previously, Turbopack knew that the named export `z` was used, but lost the static member information from expressions such as `z.object()`. Once `z` resolved to a namespace object, the optimizer therefore kept every export of `external.js` — including `locales` and all of `./locales/index.js` in this example.

The optimization must remain conservative in several cases:

- a computed property whose name cannot be determined statically, such as `z[key]`;
- a namespace binding that escapes to unknown code, such as passing `z` to another function;
- static and opaque uses of the same binding, where the opaque use must dominate narrowing;
- live exports and method calls, whose binding and receiver semantics must not change.

It must also avoid changing ordinary named-import behavior. A property read on an imported value is not proof that the value is a module namespace; narrowing and namespace provenance are valid only after re-export resolution proves that fact.

## How?

### Represent namespace-member requests explicitly

The module-part model now has explicit states for this operation:

- `ExportedNamespaceMember { export, member }` represents a static member read on a named export before re-export resolution;
- `RenamedNamespaceMember { export, member }` represents the case after that export resolves to a module namespace.

This avoids overloading an ordinary `Export` or an optional `member` field with two meanings. It also keeps existing `Export` and `RenamedNamespace` identities unchanged; the new variants have distinct hashes only for the new states.

Multiple static reads and multiple aliases are tracked as independently keyed references, so `z.object`, `z.string`, and `z.defaultLocale` all survive rather than
…(truncated)

prs.title: Fix missing content in Cached Navigations
prs.author: unstubbable
prs.body:
React can render outlined elements in later `setImmediate` callbacks after an asynchronous cache read resolves. `cacheReady()` can resolve before those elements start their cached reads. The embedded prerender for Cached Navigations then reports unexpected cache misses and omits cacheable content.

This change tracks pending native immediates in an `AsyncLocalStorage` scope around each Cache Components render. `CacheSignal` waits for that work before accepting a zero read count. If more native immediates appear before the readiness timer runs, it waits and checks again. Tracking does not make native immediates fast or change the existing explicit, task-local fast-immediate behavior.

The e2e regression uses a delayed cache handler and a large outlined tree. It verifies that Cached Navigations reuse outlined content while content behind dynamic I/O remains uncached. Each test invocation uses a fresh cache key through `searchParams`, so cases and retries cannot reuse previously warmed entries.

Unit tests in the existing immediates suite cover scope isolation, nested scheduling, cancellation, native scheduling semantics, and error recovery.

Fixes #98543

prs.title: Keep cached root parameters out of generic fallback shells
prs.author: gnoff
prs.body:
## Summary

Replace #98892 with a fix for both ways root-dependent content can enter a generic fallback shell: reusing an existing Resume Data Cache entry and executing a fresh cache fill.

For example, cached English content produced for `/en/items/one` remains reusable in `/en/items/[slug]`, but must be absent from `/[lang]/items/[slug]`. When reusing that concrete prerender as a seed, clone its cache map and replace entries whose recorded `readRootParamNames` intersect the unknown roots with omission markers. The original seed is unchanged.

Keep those markers in the cache map itself, not a separate collection that must stay synchronized. They carry the reason for a hole between prerender passes and are never serialized into the persisted RDC. Preserve canary's distinction between URL data and session data when computing shell and prefetch hints.

For fresh fills, an unknown root read suspends the entire cache invocation, including cached components with an internal Suspense boundary. Affected nested caches use independently cancellable prerenders. Dependencies propagate through consumers without cancelling independent sibling fills or saving aborted partial results.

A top-level caller joining a nested cache fill must also record the omission marker: the nested leader has no RDC of its own. Otherwise the final prerender sees an unexplained miss and loses the fallback's prefetch hint. This applies to intra-request joins as well as cross-request joins.

This is prerequisite work for configurable root fallbacks in #97393. Without the new API, ordinary misses for root parameters still block. The prerequisite fixture inspects ordinary build artifacts and document requests; the API fixtures exercise fresh fills through real fallback requests and tag invalidation. Neither uses forced rendering or shell-debugging hooks.

## Verification

- Prerequisite root-cache fixture: five production tests pass with both Webpack and freshly built Turbopack.
- API root-cache isolation and root-parameter fixtures: eleven production tests pass with each bundler. Fourteen closed-route revalidation tests also pass with Webpack after restacking.
- The new nested-leader/top-level-join regression fails without the marker write with the reported unexpected-cache-miss warning, and passes with the write. Data-service barriers determine the ordering; no timing sleeps or framework test hooks are used.
- Existing runtime prerender cache-warming coverage: eight Webpack tests pass, including cached pages that await params/searchParams.
- The three focused unit suites pass together: 114 tests on this prerequisite and 128 on the API layer, with four snapshots each. The postponed-state assertion no longer snapshots Node's incidental async-hooks fields on promises.

prs.title: Preserve closed-route admission across cache misses
prs.author: gnoff
prs.body:
## Summary

Keep route admission independent of ISR cache contents. With Cache Components disabled, a route using `dynamicParams = false` and `generateStaticParams()` can currently return 200 for a build-generated URL, then incorrectly return 404 after `revalidatePath` expires its cache entry. An empty external cache causes the same failure on the first request.

For example, if the build generated `/products/known`, that URL remains allowed after invalidation; `/products/unlisted` remains disallowed regardless of cache state. If a later build removes `/products/known`, it must immediately stop matching, even if an external cache still holds that URL's old response.

The request handler now rejects unlisted closed URLs before looking up their ISR entries. This prevents both serving an old cache hit and generating a new response for a URL the current build does not admit. An admitted build path whose matched fallback is `false` regenerates using a blocking render when necessary.

The two decisions stay separate: the manifest determines whether the URL may match, while the response generator chooses how to produce an admitted response. We do not share mutable fallback-mode state between those stages.

### Preserved exceptions and adapter behavior

- **Server Actions:** forwarding can invoke a worker at `/products/[slug]`, not a concrete page URL. Action calls retain their existing exemption from page admission checks. A retained action must still work after the user navigates away from its closed route.
- **Draft mode:** an unpublished URL can be previewed without admitting it publicly or replacing its public cache entry.
- **Minimal mode:** the platform router remains responsible for admission before invoking the renderer.
- **Adapters:** rendering a routing 404 now happens outside the response cache. The previous placement could successfully send a 404 and then throw `cache entry required but not generated` because it returned no cache entry for a non-null cache key. The new adapter fixture reproduces this on the parent runtime.

This uses the existing prerender manifest and does not change its format or the adapter contract. The most specific matched dynamic route continues to determine the policy for open URLs, so specialized matchers can admit an open suffix without admitting an unknown closed prefix.

## Regression coverage

Real fixtures cover:

- Repeated invalidation, ordinary and optional catch-all paths, time-based ISR, concurrent regeneration, and serving a stale response while regenerating in the background.
- Empty external caches and an external cache retained across two real builds. The latter verifies that the removed path's old entry still exists but is never consulted.
- Document, HEAD, navigation, prefetch, bot, rewritten, and overlapping-route requests.
- Direct and forwarded Server Actions, draft previews, and direct minimal-mode renderer invocations.

prs.title: Preserve error boundaries during on-demand prerendering
prs.author: unstubbable
prs.body:
In production, an error while generating an App Router page on demand can return a generic 500 response or a Pages Router 500 page instead of the route's `error.tsx` or `global-error.tsx`. This affects dynamic routes using `generateStaticParams`, even though their error boundaries work in development.

A completed prerender failure now carries its error and recovery output through the renderer and response cache as an explicit result. The response cache retains completed failures within each platform invocation, without changing existing in-flight batching. Failed output is not persisted as a successful ISR entry. The server sends recovered documents with status 500 and non-cacheable headers. Failed RSC responses have empty bodies; navigation falls back to loading the document. Build failures and incomplete recovery continue to throw. Asynchronous error reporting runs in the background and uses the platform's `waitUntil` when available.

Recovery that requires resuming a partially prerendered page is out of scope for this PR and continues to throw. A follow-up PR will preserve and resume that partial recovery output.

The fix applies to self-hosted production servers and adapter-based Vercel deployments. The legacy Vercel deployment path retains its existing behavior of replacing the response with a generic error page.

The tests cover both Cache Components settings, batched invocation failures, pending I/O inside Suspense, same-URL recovery, successful-page retention, and original-error reporting.

Fixes #62046

prs.title: Add experimental custom webpack support
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Add the experimental `customWebpack` configuration option so webpack-mode applications can use a project-installed webpack version instead of the version bundled with Next.js. Webpack is now an optional `^5.98.0` peer dependency, and the new option is documented with end-to-end coverage for webpack 5.98.0 and 5.111.0.

### Why?

Next.js currently redirects webpack imports to its bundled implementation. This prevents applications from opting into newer compatible webpack releases or validating upgrades independently. The new option provides an explicit escape hatch while preserving the bundled implementation as the default.

### How?

After configuration is resolved, webpack-mode startup redirects the existing webpack require-hook aliases to the package resolved from the application. The selection is propagated to webpack build workers through the existing local-webpack runtime switch. If the optional peer cannot be resolved, Next.js restores its bundled aliases and reports an actionable installation error.

The implementation only activates for webpack, leaving Turbopack and Rspack unchanged. It also handles the resolver stack API exposed by external webpack versions. The test matrix verifies the selected compiler version, rendering in development and production, the build-worker path, missing-peer diagnostics, and bundled fallback behavior when the option is disabled.

### Verification

- `pnpm test-dev-webpack test/e2e/app-dir/custom-webpack/custom-webpack.test.ts`
- `pnpm test-start-webpack test/e2e/app-dir/custom-webpack/custom-webpack.test.ts`

prs.title: [cd] Retry preview tarball uploads with backoff and richer diagnostics
prs.author: eps1lon
prs.body:
The `upload-preview-tarballs` workflow aborted its entire run when a single tarball upload hit a transient network error, and the logged error did not identify which package or request had failed. One observed run failed with `TypeError: fetch failed` (`UND_ERR_SOCKET`) after the ~78MB `next` tarball body had been written but before the response arrived (e.g. https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/35721116824/job/106724007428#step:4:19).

`scripts/upload-preview-tarballs.js` now wraps each package's upload in a retry with exponential backoff (5 attempts, 1s/2s/4s/8s). Every failure is retried, including network-level rejections without an HTTP status. Error messages now name the package and the failed request phase, and non-OK responses include a truncated response body alongside the status and response headers such as `x-vercel-id`, so the next rare failure is actionable. A package that exhausts its retries no longer aborts the remaining uploads; all failures are collected and reported at the end as an `AggregateError`.

prs.title: [ci] Skip preview tarball upload when the artifact is missing
prs.author: eps1lon
prs.body:
The build-and-deploy workflow can conclude successfully without producing a `preview-tarballs` artifact, for example when its `deploy-tarball` job is skipped on docs-only canary pushes or on production tag pushes (https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/35075211933). The `upload-preview-tarballs` workflow then failed when downloading the artifact.

This change lets the download step fail without failing the job and skips the upload step in that case, so a missing artifact no longer turns the workflow red. The failed-but-tolerated download step still leaves an error annotation on the green run. Real breakage still surfaces in build-and-test, which waits on the published tarballs.
